evaluationApproach.summary: The AI must evaluate each answer specifically for a Mental Coach working in soccer. It should assess evidence-informed mental-performance practice, soccer application, developmental appropriateness, ethical boundaries, collaboration, impact measurement and referral judgment. It must not assume that a mental coach is a licensed clinical psychologist.
evaluationApproach.corePrinciple: A strong answer demonstrates practical performance support while protecting player autonomy, confidentiality, safety and clinical boundaries. Confidence or motivational language cannot replace qualifications, process and ethical judgment.

mandatoryRules.rule: Score against Mental Coach expectations, not Mental Coach, therapist, psychologist or general Office Staff criteria.
Do not infer clinical licensure, protected titles or authority from confidence, certificates or self-description.
For questions requesting a real example, do not award 4/4 without the situation, action and outcome.
Reward evidence-informed, individualized and soccer-relevant practice rather than motivational language alone.
A clinically concerning disclosure should trigger referral or safeguarding procedures, not diagnosis by the scoring AI.
Flag contradictions between questionnaire and video, but do not treat contradiction alone as proof of dishonesty.
Do not reward promises of guaranteed confidence, selection, recovery, performance or mental-health outcomes.
Do not score accent, grammar, appearance, age, gender, ethnicity, disability or production quality. Evaluate content.

calibrationOverall.classification: Basic / acceptable; evidence or depth is limited
calibrationOverall.strongestAreas: Soccer-specific preparation routines; role boundaries; autonomy and respectful collaboration
calibrationOverall.mainWeaknesses: Assessment validity; safeguarding details; structured measurement and follow-up evidence
calibrationOverall.summary: The candidate demonstrates a reasonable understanding of soccer-specific mental-performance support, particularly attention routines, autonomy and clinical boundaries. However, several answers lack structured assessment, consent documentation, safeguarding detail and measurable follow-up. Additional evidence is needed to verify qualifications, confidentiality procedures, intervention outcomes and referral readiness.

questions.text: Can you describe your background and training in mental performance or sport psychology?
questions.evaluates: Relevant education, supervised experience, credentials and scope awareness.
strong: Clearly distinguishes formal education, certifications, supervised practice and continuing development.
Connects training to evidence-informed mental-performance work.
Accurately states professional scope and does not imply clinical licensure that is not held.
questions.acceptable: Describes relevant training and experience but provides limited detail about supervision, application or scope.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Relies only on personal experience or motivational ability, misrepresents credentials, or claims authority to diagnose or treat without appropriate qualification.

calibration.response: I completed a sport-performance coaching course and have worked with academy players on focus routines. I am not a clinical psychologist.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Relevant scope awareness and experience; supervision, specific qualifications and practical outcomes remain unclear.

questions.text: What is your experience working with soccer players or team staff specifically?
questions.evaluates: Soccer-context experience and understanding of the performance environment.
strong: Describes specific age groups, levels, roles and forms of intervention.
Understands soccer demands such as selection, errors, playing time, injury, team hierarchy and match pressure.
Explains collaboration and outcomes without breaching confidentiality.
questions.acceptable: Shows relevant athlete or team experience but limited soccer-specific depth.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Provides only generic wellness experience, name-drops clients, or discloses identifiable confidential information.

calibration.response: I supported youth soccer players during trial periods and helped them create routines after mistakes.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Relevant soccer setting and intervention; limited detail about ages, staff coordination and observed change.

questions.text: How do you define the role of a mental coach within a soccer environment?
questions.evaluates: Role clarity, performance contribution and ethical boundaries.
strong: Defines development of mental skills, self-regulation, learning and performance habits.
Supports players and staff while respecting coaching, medical and clinical responsibilities.
Explains consent, confidentiality, safeguarding and referral boundaries.
questions.acceptable: Defines mental-skills support and performance preparation but gives incomplete boundary detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Presents the role as therapy, diagnosis, team discipline, guaranteed performance improvement or motivational speaking alone.

calibration.response: I help players develop concentration and confidence while referring mental-health concerns to qualified professionals.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Appropriate role definition and referral boundary; consent, confidentiality and safeguarding process are underdeveloped.

questions.text: What is your general methodology when working with players (individual vs collective)?
questions.evaluates: Coherent, flexible and evidence-informed intervention design.
strong: Begins with needs, context, goals and informed agreement rather than a fixed program.
Explains appropriate individual and group formats, confidentiality limits and stakeholder roles.
Uses a cycle of assessment, intervention, practice, feedback and review.
questions.acceptable: Describes individual and group work with reasonable activities but limited process or review detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Applies one fixed method to all players or shares individual disclosures in group settings.

calibration.response: I meet players individually to discuss goals and run group workshops on preparation, then review how they feel.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Basic individual and group approach; missing informed agreement, structured intervention cycle and review indicators.

questions.text: How do you assess a player's mental profile at the start of your work?
questions.evaluates: Responsible assessment, interpretation and avoidance of unsupported profiling.
strong: Uses interview, observation, performance context, self-report and validated tools when qualified to use them.
Explains consent, purpose, limitations, cultural context and secure handling of information.
Treats the profile as a working hypothesis and establishes measurable goals with the player.
questions.acceptable: Uses conversation and questionnaires to identify needs but gives limited validity or privacy detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Diagnoses from a brief questionnaire, labels personality as fixed, uses unvalidated tests as fact, or shares results without consent.

calibration.response: I ask about pressure situations and use a short self-report questionnaire to understand their needs.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Useful initial discussion but limited tool validity, consent, privacy and contextual interpretation.

questions.text: Which mental skills do you prioritize most in soccer (e.g. confidence, focus, resilience, emotional control), and why?
questions.evaluates: Prioritization based on player and performance demands.
strong: Avoids a universal ranking and links priorities to role, age, context and identified needs.
Explains relevant skills such as attentional control, confidence, emotional regulation, coping and communication.
Connects each skill to observable soccer behavior and trainable routines.
questions.acceptable: Names relevant mental skills and gives general soccer reasons.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Selects skills based only on personal preference, uses vague concepts, or promises elimination of normal emotions.

calibration.response: I focus on attention and coping with mistakes because players must reset quickly after losing the ball.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Soccer-relevant priorities and rationale; lacks individual selection criteria and concrete training progression.

questions.text: How do you adapt your work according to age groups (youth, academy, senior players)?
questions.evaluates: Developmental appropriateness, safeguarding and contextual adaptation.
strong: Adjusts language, session length, autonomy, examples and expectations to development stage.
Explains safeguarding, parental or guardian involvement and confidentiality limits for minors.
Recognizes different identity, education, selection, contract and transition pressures.
questions.acceptable: Adapts communication and exercises by age but gives limited safeguarding or developmental detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Uses adult methods unchanged with children, excludes required safeguarding, or promises confidentiality beyond lawful and safety limits.

calibration.response: With younger players I use short games and simple language; with senior players I use more detailed reflection.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Age-appropriate adaptation is identified; safeguarding, guardians and confidentiality limits are not addressed.

questions.text: How do you handle pressure-related issues such as competition stress, selection anxiety, or fear of failure?
questions.evaluates: Applied coping support, normalization and appropriate escalation.
strong: Assesses triggers, intensity, function, context and effect on performance.
Uses appropriate skills such as preparation routines, breathing, attention cues, reframing, exposure or reflection.
Normalizes pressure, tracks response and refers when symptoms exceed scope or indicate risk.
questions.acceptable: Offers relevant coping strategies and follow-up but gives limited assessment or referral detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Dismisses distress, guarantees anxiety removal, uses punishment or pressure, or treats severe symptoms outside competence.

calibration.response: We identify stressful moments, practice breathing and use a simple reset cue during training.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Plausible practical routine; intensity assessment, monitoring and escalation pathways need more detail.

questions.text: Can you give an example of how you prepare a player mentally for an important match or trial?
questions.evaluates: Practical preparation, individualization and transfer to performance.
strong: Provides a specific situation, identified need and collaborative plan.
Uses realistic routines, controllable goals, attention cues and scenario rehearsal integrated with normal preparation.
Explains implementation, outcome and learning without claiming certainty or guaranteed selection.
questions.acceptable: Provides a relevant preparation routine but limited individualization or outcome evidence.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Relies only on motivational speeches, introduces unfamiliar techniques immediately before the event, or promises a result.

calibration.response: Before a trial, I asked a winger to choose two controllable goals and practice a reset cue in training. The player reported feeling more prepared afterward.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Specific context, routine and self-report outcome; lacks systematic follow-up and independent behavioral evidence.

questions.text: How do you collaborate with coaches, technical staff, and medical staff?
questions.evaluates: Interdisciplinary collaboration, consent and information boundaries.
strong: Clarifies roles, referral routes, meeting cadence and shared performance objectives.
Obtains appropriate consent and shares only necessary, agreed information.
Coordinates support while preserving player trust and escalating safety concerns appropriately.
questions.acceptable: Communicates with staff and aligns support but gives limited consent or information-sharing detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Shares private session content routinely, works in isolation, overrides medical decisions or becomes a source of team surveillance.

calibration.response: I speak with coaches about general performance goals and keep individual conversations private unless there is a safety concern.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Good confidentiality instincts and collaboration; consent procedures and referral coordination remain unspecified.

questions.text: How do you ensure your mental coaching aligns with the team's game model and performance objectives?
questions.evaluates: Integration of mental skills with football behaviors and team demands.
strong: Clarifies game principles and identifies related mental demands in training and matches.
Embeds cues, routines and reflection into football tasks rather than separating all mental work.
Balances team objectives with individual welfare and avoids using psychology to enforce unquestioning compliance.
questions.acceptable: Connects mental skills to team objectives but gives limited behavioral or integration detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Uses generic motivation unrelated to the game model or treats mental coaching as a tool to control players.

calibration.response: I link attention cues to the team pressing and transition principles and practice them on the field.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Clear connection between mental skills and soccer actions; little detail on checking transfer or balancing welfare.

questions.text: What boundaries do you set between mental coaching and clinical psychology?
questions.evaluates: Scope of practice, referral judgment and safety.
strong: Clearly distinguishes performance coaching from diagnosis and treatment of mental disorders.
Recognizes warning signs, crisis procedures, safeguarding duties and referral pathways to licensed clinicians.
Explains confidentiality and its limits, documentation, consent and coordinated care.
questions.acceptable: Recognizes that clinical issues require referral but gives limited process detail.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Claims to treat clinical disorders without proper credentials, discourages clinical care, promises absolute confidentiality or lacks a crisis/referral process.

calibration.response: I do not diagnose mental disorders. If I notice serious concerns, I recommend a licensed clinician and follow club safeguarding procedures.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Appropriate scope distinction; missing detailed risk-response steps, consent and documentation.

questions.text: How do you measure the effectiveness of your mental coaching work?
questions.evaluates: Ethical outcome measurement and understanding of contribution versus causation.
strong: Sets collaborative goals and uses multiple indicators such as self-report, observable routines, behavior, adherence and stakeholder feedback.
Uses baselines, periodic review and contextual interpretation.
Avoids claiming that mental coaching alone caused match results or selection outcomes.
questions.acceptable: Uses player feedback and behavioral or performance indicators but lacks a structured baseline or review process.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Measures success only through wins, goals or testimonials, or guarantees direct causal impact.

calibration.response: I ask players to rate confidence before and after a program and gather feedback from coaches.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Basic outcome measures; no clear baseline design, behavior indicators, periodic review or attribution caution.

questions.text: Can you share an example of a situation where your intervention had a clear impact on performance or behavior?
questions.evaluates: Applied impact, evidence and appropriate attribution.
strong: Provides the situation, goal, intervention, observed change and follow-up.
Protects identity and confidentiality while giving enough evidence to assess contribution.
Acknowledges other influences, uncertainty and lessons learned.
questions.acceptable: Provides a relevant example but lacks baseline, follow-up or clarity about contribution.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Reveals a player's identity or sensitive information, claims sole credit, or provides an unsupported success story.

calibration.response: One player used a pre-match routine and reported feeling calmer after several weeks.
calibration.label: Acceptable
calibration.assessment: Plausible change but limited baseline, intervention detail, follow-up and evidence of contribution.

questions.text: How do you adapt your approach when a player is resistant or not fully engaged?
questions.evaluates: Autonomy support, alliance-building and adaptive practice.
strong: Explores reasons for resistance without labeling or coercion.
Revisits consent, goals, readiness, format, cultural factors and the player's preferred level of involvement.
Adjusts methods, respects refusal, documents appropriately and refers or pauses when needed.
questions.acceptable: Uses listening and method adjustment but gives limited attention to consent or stopping criteria.
questions.weakOrConcerning: Forces participation, reports resistance as disobedience, manipulates selection pressure or breaches confidentiality to gain compliance.

calibration.response: I listen to why the player is hesitant, offer a different exercise and do not force participation.
calibration.label: Good
calibration.assessment: Respects autonomy and adapts approach; could better explain consent review, stopping criteria and documentation.
